strengths: UniAP addresses a useful infrastructure problem by jointly selecting pipeline placement and DP, TP, and FSDP strategies under resource constraints. The ViT and Swin experiments establish relevance to training large vision models.

Table 2 demonstrates meaningful throughput improvements: on ENV_B, UniAP exceeds the stronger reported baseline by 1.18× for ViT and 1.37× for Swin; LLaMA improves by 1.61× on ENV_C. These are worthwhile practical results.

Search-time reductions provide value even when training throughput matches Galvatron. For example, BERT on ENV_A retains the same throughput while reducing optimization time from 6.44 to 0.37 minutes. UniAP also finds a working Swin configuration where Galvatron encounters CUDA OOM.

The evaluation includes five model families, several hardware configurations, a throughput-prediction check, and a topology-aware case study. Hardware specifications, model dimensions, and solver settings provide useful implementation detail.
weaknesses: The placement constraints have a material correctness gap. Equations (6a–c) enforce contiguity but do not order pipeline stages. For a two-layer chain u→v, placing u on stage 2 and v on stage 1 satisfies these constraints, yet Equation (4) assigns zero communication cost because it counts only edges from stage j to j+1. Consequently, the stated optimization admits undercosted solutions. Appendix A proves contiguity without resolving this issue.

The advertised MIQP is not supplied in a directly reproducible form. Equations (3) and (4) contain products such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v), which are quartic in the decision variables. Auxiliary variables could reformulate these terms, but the manuscript does not provide that transformation or its constraints. This is a correctable specification omission, although it matters substantially for reproducing the central solver and its reported runtime.

GPipe activation-memory accounting is insufficiently specified. Algorithm 1 constructs M using micro-batch size b=B/c, while Equation (5) includes no explicit accumulation across micro-batches. Without checkpointing, GPipe retains activations from multiple forward micro-batches before their backward passes. The described calculation can therefore underestimate peak memory unless an unreported correction is applied. Throughput-prediction accuracy does not validate this feasibility constraint.

The repeated claims of finding an optimal strategy exceed the evidence. Appendix D permits a 60-second timeout and termination after 15 seconds with an optimality gap below 4%, but achieved gaps and termination statuses are not reported. Moreover, any solver guarantee concerns the restricted candidates and approximate cost model. The polynomial complexity claim in Section 3.5 relies on fixing the solver timeout; it does not establish the complexity of obtaining an optimal solution.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed advantage of joint optimization over hierarchical optimization. Figure 7 removes either inter-layer or intra-layer parallelism entirely, rather than comparing joint and hierarchical searches using the same candidates, cost model, and execution backend. The MFU comparison in Appendix E also cannot isolate strategy-space effects because execution efficiency influences MFU.

The optimization-time comparison measures a narrower benefit than total setup efficiency: profiling is excluded, and Section 4.1 attributes part of the advantage to multithreaded Gurobi versus single-threaded baselines. Matched CPU budgets and a breakdown of preparation costs are missing. Overall, the measured systems benefits are promising, but the unresolved formulation and memory-feasibility gaps make the current balance favor weak rejection.
